facts: In early 1962 NASA prepared to launch John Glenn into orbit around the Earth.
The trajectory calculations used a new electronic computer, which many on the team did not yet trust.
Glenn asked that Katherine Johnson check the computer's figures by hand before he would fly.
Johnson worked at NASA's Langley research centre as a mathematician; she had come from the segregated group of Black women who did calculations.
She checked the figures and Glenn flew; the launch and three orbits succeeded in February 1962.

Gagarin orbited in 1961; Johnson had computed Shepard's 1961 trajectory; her unit was West Area Computing under Dorothy Vaughan; Mary Jackson worked there; Johnson was 43; capsule Friendship 7; flight ~5 hours.

opening_idea: Open on John Glenn asking for one person to check the computer's figures before he would launch.

lessons.idea: Trust is earned by work that proves right again and again, and it surfaces when the stakes rise.
lessons.anchor: Glenn asked for Katherine Johnson's check

reflect_final: Whose numbers or judgement do you rely on when it truly matters, and what have they done to earn it?

use_cases.situation: You want to be the person others turn to.
use_cases.move: Show your working on the next task so it can be checked.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Before John Glenn would orbit the Earth, he asked for Katherine Johnson to check the computer's numbers.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In 1962 NASA planned to launch John Glenn into orbit, with the trajectory figures calculated by a new electronic computer. Glenn asked for Katherine Johnson, a Langley mathematician, to check the numbers by hand first. She did, and he flew. Margot Lee Shetterly tells this in Hidden Figures about the Black women whose work stood behind the launch.
